title: Prompt Injection Defenses Fall Apart in Long Context
hook: Injection benchmarks are all short-context, which has been flattering the defenses. Stretch the input to tens of thousands of tokens and even naive attacks walk through state-of-the-art protections.
key_points: Existing prompt injection benchmarks focus on short inputs, leaving long-context attacks and defenses unexplored.
The authors argue this gap substantially overestimates how effective current defenses are.
LongPIBench covers four realistic scenarios: paper peer review, resume screening, code review, and email summary.
Each scenario has a synthetic and a real-world dataset, with contexts from thousands to tens of thousands of tokens.
Even simple heuristic injection attacks achieve high success rates and frequently bypass state-of-the-art defenses.
content_html: Prompt injection is the security problem of the LLM application era, and the field has a benchmark suite for it. Liu and colleagues point out that suite is almost entirely short-context — which means the reassuring numbers defenses report may not describe the settings people actually deploy in.
extra_html:
The benchmark

LongPIBench covers four scenarios chosen because they are both realistic and long: paper peer review, resume screening, code review, and email summarization. Each has a synthetic dataset and a real-world one, with context lengths from thousands to tens of thousands of tokens.

The finding

Defenses degrade badly. The authors report that even simple heuristic injection attacks achieve high success rates and frequently bypass state-of-the-art defenses at these lengths. That is the uncomfortable part: it does not take an adaptive adversary or an optimized suffix, just a longer document to hide in.

Why it matters

Long context is not an exotic configuration — it is the default for exactly the workflows in this benchmark, where an LLM reads a large untrusted document and acts on it. If defense evaluations have all been run at a length where the injected text is a big fraction of the prompt, the reported protection is measuring the easy case. This is a benchmark-gap paper, and its main claim is about the evaluation practice as much as about any particular defense.

related.title: When Tool Outputs Become Commands
related.hook: Prompt injection into agents is really one confusion: the thing that suggests an action and the thing that authorizes it are treated as the same thing.

related.title: Stacked Defenses Only Multiply If They Fail Independently
related.hook: A seven-layer defense stack refuses four in five benign prompts and is statistically indistinguishable from its single best layer — because the layers all fail on the same inputs.

flashcards.prompt: Why did short-context benchmarks overestimate prompt injection defenses?
flashcards.back_html: Defenses that work when the injected text is a large fraction of a short prompt lose their grip when it is buried in tens of thousands of tokens of legitimate content.

choices.text: Even simple heuristic attacks frequently bypass state-of-the-art defenses in long context
Long context makes injection strictly harder for the attacker
Only gradient-based adaptive attacks succeed at long context lengths

flashcards.explanation_html: The point is how little sophistication is needed. If naive attacks work at length, reported defense effectiveness from short-context evaluations does not transfer.
